data.title: Federal Reserve policymakers concerned about financial system risks, minutes show
data.description:
[NEW YORK] Financial stability risks tied to aggressive artificial intelligence investment and elevated asset prices are on the US central bank’s radar, the minutes from the Federal Reserve’s policy meeting last month showed on Wednesday (Nov 18).

The concern was raised as part of a broad review of financial risks by Fed policymakers and central bank staff at the Oct 27-28 policy meeting.

That gathering saw officials hold interest rates steady despite ongoing worries about high and persistent levels of inflation. However, “almost all” policymakers agreed that further hikes would be needed if the economy evolved as they expected, the minutes showed.

“The staff judged that current vulnerabilities could amplify shocks somewhat more than usual, with elevated asset valuations and leverage at hedge funds representing the most salient vulnerabilities, while strong bank and household balance sheets provided an important buffer against more severe outcomes,” the minutes said.

Policymakers expressed concern that huge levels of investment in AI technology could lead to trouble and create broader problems for both the financial system and economy.

“Almost all participants commented on risks associated with a scenario in which the returns on AI investment turned out to be disappointing to investors,” the minutes said.

“Most participants observed that AI-related debt had grown rapidly and that much of this growth had taken place through complex and opaque financing structures,” while “a few” of the unnamed Fed officials were concerned that AI exposure was being concentrated in a “small number” of companies.

Fed officials also cast an anxious eye toward hedge funds.

“Most participants highlighted hedge fund leverage or limited dealer intermediation capacity as potential channels of amplification during periods of market stress,” the minutes said.

Fed staff described the financial system as “resilient,” with banks having ample access to cash, according to the minutes. But some policymakers worried that “banking system vulnerabilities could emerge rapidly even after seemingly reassuring initial assessments.”

Some were also worried the Fed‘s data on the banking system may miss the full range of exposure some financial firms have.

Building resilience

Financial markets have been under stress in recent weeks amid questions about the future of AI and how the buildout of the technology has increasingly come to rely on debt. Past periods of financial trouble have been frequently associated with excessive borrowing, and some of those crises have driven the Fed to intervene to stabilise markets.

The latest minutes also showed Fed officials weighing how they can respond to future troubles.

“A few” policymakers mulled boosting banks’ capital levels while some also said it is important to better prepare banks to use the Fed‘s emergency lending discount window facility, which is something officials have been working on for some time.

In addition, “a few” policymakers considered a novel strategy in which the Fed would set up a dedicated method of asset-buying that would explicitly target financial stability concerns.

The Fed is weighing the future of how it uses its balance sheet as a policy tool. Fed holdings have swollen massively over the last two decades due to huge bond purchases during the 2008 global financial crisis and the Covid-19 pandemic.

The pandemic experience has loomed particularly large because bond-buying that began in March 2020 started out as a stabilisation tool that morphed into outright stimulus.

Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack is among those who would like to see a more clearly defined system for buying bonds that would also entail a strategy to sell them when a crisis has passed.

Hammack said earlier this week that any programme “should also be temporary, and holdings should be sold in a timely way once market financial stability is restored.”

The minutes noted that “several” policymakers cautioned that monetary policy is not the right tool to deal with market trouble. But the large role now played by AI and technology investment in driving economic growth might complicate that view if large-scale problems emerged. REUTERS

data.title: Stocks to watch: SIA, Olam, F&N
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Tuesday (Nov 17):

Singapore Airlines (SIA) : The national carrier reported a 3.5 per cent rise in passenger traffic in October from the year-ago period amid “resilient” demand for air travel. SIA and its budget arm Scoot carried 3.7 million passengers during the month, up 4.5 per cent from a year ago. The group’s October passenger capacity concurrently rose 2.9 per cent, while the passenger load factor was up 0.5 percentage point at 87.8 per cent. Shares of SIA rose 0.8 per cent or S$0.06 to close at S$7.22 on Monday.

Olam : The agreement made by the agribusiness to sell its 32.4 per cent stake in port and logistics operator Arise P&L for US$175 million was terminated on Nov 15 as certain conditions of the deal were not fulfilled, it said in a bourse filing on Monday. Olam entered into a sale and purchase agreement with Dubai-based investment platform Equitane DMCC in April 2025 and expected the sale to close in FY2025. Shares of Olam ended Monday at S$0.845, down 1.7 per cent or S$0.015.

F&N : The beverage maker posted an 8.3 per cent year-on-year increase in net profit to S$63 million for the second half ended September, as its beverages business recovered and Vietnamese dairy associate Vinamilk contributed more to earnings. The board proposed a final dividend of S$0.04, unchanged from the previous year. Shares of F&N ended Monday flat at S$1.34.

data.title: Anthropic prices blockbuster IPO at US$83 a share: source
data.description:
ANTHROPIC priced its initial public offering at US$83 a share, above its targeted range of US$70 to US$78 per share on Wednesday (Nov 18), in one of the largest stock-market IPOs on record and the first by a major frontier artificial intelligence model developer, according to a person familiar with the matter.

The size of the offering has increased, the person said, asking not to be identified because the information isn’t public. Anthropic initially planned to sell 825 million shares.

Anthropic‘s sale is the second mega-IPO this year focused on AI, following June’s SpaceX sale, as investors jump at the chance for exposure to the fast-growing industry, even as the industry also faces mounting questions over the cost of developing and operating artificial intelligence models.

The AI lab comes to the public market just months after SpaceX’s record-setting IPO, even as the backdrop for AI stocks has turned more challenging.

Chipmakers and cloud companies central to the business have come under pressure in recent weeks due to valuation concerns, mounting AI infrastructure costs, and the sudden resignation of Jensen Huang as CEO of chipmaker Nvidia, a key pillar of the industry’s growth.

The pricing follows a roadshow that attracted demand several times the number of shares offered, Reuters previously reported, despite questions about the company’s outlook and its ability to sustain rapid growth as competition in the AI industry intensifies.

Anthropic‘s closest rival, OpenAI, is also expected to pursue a public listing as early as next year.

Anthropic declined to comment.

Bloomberg News first reported on the pricing.

Anthropic‘s growth has been driven by surging demand for its Claude models, particularly Claude Code, its coding agent that has gained popularity among software developers. Its annualised revenue run rate reached US$81 billion as of Oct 31, up US$10 billion from Sep 30, according to its IPO filing.

The Claude maker said it had 11,900 customers generating at least US$100,000 in annual revenue on a trailing 12-month basis as of Sep 30, compared with more than 1,500 at the end of last year, underscoring its growing business foothold.

But sustaining that growth is becoming expensive. Anthropic spent nearly US$9 billion on computing capacity and infrastructure in the first half of 2026, nearly four times the amount spent a year earlier. It also incurred an additional US$5 billion in computing costs in the third quarter, weighing on efficiency and reducing the revenue generated per dollar of computing capacity.

Revenue rose 47 per cent in the third quarter to US$16.96 billion. The company reported an operating loss of US$567 million, compared with operating income of US$974 million in the second quarter. Net ⁠loss fell ​to US$23.3 billion from US$66.3 billion a quarter earlier, including non-operating ​items related to bonds convertible into its shares.

Anthropic has committed to nearly US$900 billion in computing spending with infrastructure partners including Amazon and Alphabet’s Google, part of its ongoing expenditures to train and operate increasingly powerful AI models.

Its spending commitments also expose the company to risks beyond its own finances.

Anthropic warned in its prospectus that some of its computing providers and infrastructure partners depend on third-party financing and credit support to acquire chips and build capacity. “If such financing or support becomes unavailable or more costly, contracted capacity may be delayed, repriced, reduced, or not delivered,” Anthropic said in an IPO filing.

Investors have grown increasingly concerned about debt-fuelled expansion of AI infrastructure, with technology companies and data-centre operators borrowing heavily to finance chips, power and computing facilities.

Anthropic also faces questions over how it will balance its commercial ambitions with its emphasis on AI safety. CEO Dario Amodei has called for the industry to slow the pace of developing and releasing increasingly powerful models, warning that advances in AI could outstrip society’s ability to manage the risks.

Shares are expected to start trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker ANT.

Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are the lead underwriters for Anthropic‘s offering, which has a 22-bank underwriting syndicate. The two banks also served as lead underwriters for SpaceX’s IPO earlier this year. REUTERS

data.title: Stocks to watch: Jardine Matheson, Riverstone, Deluge
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Wednesday (Nov 18):

Jardine Matheson: The Hong Kong-based conglomerate expects to post a 2026 dividend of at least US$2.50 per share, amid “strong performance” for the third quarter ended Sep 30. This comes after Jardine Matheson raised its full-year profit guidance in October to between US$5.50 and US$5.65 per share on an underlying basis, from the previous guidance of US$5.33 per share. For Q3, its Indonesian unit Astra International’s underlying net profit rose 11 per cent. Shares of Jardine Matheson closed 1 per cent or US$0.62 lower at US$59.15 on Tuesday, before the news.

Riverstone : The glove maker posted a 34.7 per cent rise in net profit to RM70.1 million (US$17.1 million) for the third quarter ended September. Riverstone’s Q3 revenue rose 27.3 per cent to RM315.1 million, marking the group’s highest quarterly revenue in over three years. It also announced that CEO Wong Teek Son will step down on Dec 1, to be succeeded by Chong Chu Mee. Riverstone shares closed 2.1 per cent or S$0.015 higher at S$0.745 on Tuesday, before the results.

Deluge : The fire detection and protection company has secured S$18.5 million in new contracts across Singapore and Malaysia, bringing its cumulative contract wins since January 2026 to more than S$147.7 million. The latest awards span infrastructure, marine and offshore, residential and industrial projects, including a Penang data centre project. Shares of Deluge closed 0.8 per cent or S$0.005 lower at S$0.605 on Tuesday.

data.title: Trumpâs America remains a less welcoming place for talent and foreign students
data.description:
FOR THOUSANDS of students across Asia, Singapore included, the US is the top choice for tertiary education – if they have the means or the funding.

Britain and Australia follow. Those who look to eventually immigrate will likely add Canada as a fourth prospect, for both quality education and a possible future home.

Those still eyeing the US as the land of learning and lucre will probably need to wait until US President Donald Trump finishes his term in early 2029.

Even as critics savour the Republican Party’s setbacks in the US midterms, there is little sign Washington will soften its stance on immigration.

Trump recognises that immigration was an important issue for voters.

But even as he acknowledged that the excesses of his immigration policy had hurt him, and made cursory mention of working with Democrats on this, his interview with CBS’ 60 Minutes showed no indication that he intends to abandon his administration’s overall hostility towards immigration.

And, shortly after the interview, he walked off to announce that immigration hardliner Stephen Miller would replace Susie Wiles as his chief of staff, the most influential unelected position in the White House.

“An accelerant of executive power”

Miller, the grand vizier of Trump’s Maga (Make America Great Again) politics, will get his way. Through the Trump presidency, he has focused on immigration and hardline domestic issues. Migrants, in his view, are “invaders”.

Friends and foes alike think Miller is an “accelerant of executive power” – shorthand for an operator who will unbridledly leverage the weight and power of the presidency to not only fulfil his superior’s agenda, but also his own. 

Unlike Trump’s Cabinet members, who can be impeached by Congress, only one man can unseat him: the President himself. Proximity is power.

Hence, few buy into Trump’s talk of working with Democrats on the issue.

Trump himself had previously spoken of working with the opposition on immigration, and nothing came of it. 

Cooperation across the aisle is even less likely now, as Democrats, who won every congressional district on the US-Mexico border during the midterms, see the battle lines being drawn with Miller’s appointment.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer described the Miller appointment as “not a course correction, (but) a promotion”. For Hakeem Jeffries, House Democratic leader, Miller is a “stone-cold racist”.

Will Trump chicken out – as he frequently does?

Unlikely when it concerns domestic political issues. The exception is when the financial markets come into play, as seen in his unsuccessful attempt to pressure former US Federal Reserve chairman Jerome Powell to quit, after threats to fire him.

To Trump, a setback to his agenda is usually just another opportunity to effect a workaround.

Look at what he did after the Supreme Court, in a 6-3 decision this June, struck down an executive order limiting birthright citizenship. Just over a month later, he issued two narrower orders targeting the same issue.

The brazenness has worked for him for the most part. How many men do you know got re-elected to the world’s most powerful office six months after being convicted of 34 felony counts, and while awaiting formal sentencing?

Limits of congressional checks

Those awaiting a softer American line on immigration would be prudent to expect disappointment.

The Republican Party is unlikely to pressure Trump on the matter, despite its recent electoral setbacks that saw control of Congress pass into Democratic hands.

See what they just did for Pete Hegseth, Trump’s secretary of war.

The Republican House majority – which will vanish when the new members are sworn in come January – rallied to save him from impeachment, at a time when the war on Iran is even more unpopular with Americans than immigration.

Ordinarily, with Congress passing into Democratic hands, the legislature could be expected to exercise more oversight of presidential policy by controlling the budgetary purse strings. But on immigration policy, Trump is insulated from those handcuffs.

The Secure America Act that he signed in June funds immigration enforcement through September 2029.

The bulk of the money is allocated to Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, to fund its operations and mass deportations. Even border enforcement – for which Trump claimed voters gave him much credit – is lower in the budgetary provisions.

Democrats looking to bring about changes to immigration policy had declined to back further funding for ICE and Border Patrol.

But the House voted 214-212, with the measure passing in June solely on Republican strength, and Trump quickly signed it into law.

The overwhelming prioritisation of enforcement funding is happening without additional funding to Citizenship and Immigration Services to process visas and other services. In many Asian countries, the wait for a US visa interview can take weeks or even months.

A changed mood

The harder reality to stomach is that Trump’s tougher stance on immigration may not be too far out of step with a changed national mood.

In the US Midwest particularly, such creeping hostility to foreign-born migrants is causing a steady exodus towards coastal metropolises like New York and San Francisco.

An Asia-born senior legal counsel told me a few months ago that he and his wife, a doctor, moved from Milwaukee to the West Coast after they learnt that even their friendly neighbours had taken to referring to them as the “Huxtables” – after a fictional upwardly mobile black American family that moves into a predominantly white neighbourhood.

That story was the premise of the 1980s sitcom The Cosby Show.

In my two trips to the US in the past 14 months – entering through New York and San Francisco, two of its most global cities – I experienced a longer than usual chat with an immigration officer.

Never before had I felt uneasy entering this country admired by many. I need to be there again next June for a family event, and have found myself already scouting for credible excuses not to go.

That palpable sense of apprehension among foreign visitors may be one reason why inbound tourism numbers remain below pre-pandemic levels.

Furthermore, international tourist arrivals fell 5.5 per cent in 2025 compared with the 72.3 million visitors the US received in 2024, according to the US Travel Association. In 2026, that number is expected to decline further.

And so it is for foreign students, too. US education data suggests that in the first full year of Trump’s second stint as president, new international student enrolments fell by 17 per cent.

Nearly 16,000 fewer foreign students vied for spots at US colleges in 2026 than in 2025, CommonApp, the most widely used college application platform, reported in August, following tighter visa rules and heightened restrictions on overseas arrivals.

Miller’s significant influence on immigration policy

At 41 – roughly half his boss’ age – Miller has plenty of runway left.

Born and raised though he was in liberal California, and himself a descendant of Eastern European Jewish immigrants, he has enjoyed a meteoric rise since leaving Duke University to work for Tea Party firebrand Michele Bachmann.

He is unlikely to relent in advancing the agenda of a US president who recently awarded himself an “A-plus” for closing the border. And he can be trusted to do his utmost to delay the projected trend of non-Hispanic white Americans becoming a minority between 2041 and 2045.

But it would be a mistake to think this shift in political direction is cost-free. Already, talent is turning away from the US, thanks to Trumpian policies – led by Chinese and Indians heading home to tech hubs such as Shenzhen and Bengaluru, as well as emerging hubs such as Dubai.

Whether Miller succeeds in reshaping America’s long-term trajectory is another question. For all its political turbulence, America does have a habit of self-correcting.

Bachmann, herself the big star of conservative politics in 2009, had flamed out by 2013, a period that included a failed presidential bid.

In 2015, she left Congress and has since been on the faculty of Regent University – a niche Christian institution far removed from the mainstream destinations that draw top foreign students.

Now, how many famous political or business leaders can you recall came from Regent? THE STRAITS TIMES

data.title: Oil prices settle lower as traders weigh surplus supply outlook
data.description:
[HOUSTON] Oil prices settled down more than 1 per cent on Wednesday (Nov 18) after US crude and fuel inventories posted larger-than-expected rises, according to the Energy Information Administration, adding to expectations of a supply surplus.

Brent crude futures settled down US$1.19, or 1.28 per cent, at US$91.95 a barrel. US West Texas Intermediate futures settled down US$2.75, or 3.2 per cent, at US$83.26, their lowest since Aug 26.

Brent fell more than US$2 a barrel during the session, while WTI lost more than US$4.

US crude inventories rose by 3.4 million barrels to 417.8 million barrels in the week ended Nov 13, the EIA said, compared with analysts’ expectations in a Reuters poll for a rise of 58,000 barrels.

US petrol stocks rose by 5.2 million barrels in the week to 215.9 million barrels, the EIA said, compared with analysts’ expectations in a Reuters poll for a build of 1.6 million barrels.​

Distillate stockpiles, which include diesel and heating oil, rose by 1.6 million barrels in the week to 104.9 million barrels, versus expectations for a rise of 1.3 million barrels, the EIA data showed.

Those stock increases renewed selling pressure, Gelber & Associates analysts said, adding: “Attacks involving Iran and commercial shipping still threaten deliveries through the Strait of Hormuz, but those risks have provided limited support against the growing expectation of a global surplus.”

Meanwhile, both Brent and US crude futures contracts were on track for declines of about 20 per cent this month on rising exports from the Middle East, as signalled by plummeting shipping rates.

The Brent/WTI spread was trading at its widest in around two weeks on Tuesday, LSEG data showed, with WTI logging steeper declines during trading on Wednesday.

“WTI arbitrage trades have been shut to Asia and North-west Europe, thus WTI correcting more than Brent is the expected price movement to allow the arbitrage window to open again,” said June Goh at Sparta Commodities, adding that rising US Gulf Coast crude stocks are further contributing to the widening spread.

US-Iran conflict continues

But the continuing Iran war and the risks to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz curbed price declines.

Iran said it attacked US drone and missile sites in Kuwait overnight after the US struck Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz. It was Iran’s first attack on the US-allied Gulf state since September. Bahrain, home of the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet, said it intercepted Iranian attacks.

Both oil benchmarks had settled higher on Tuesday as attacks on ships in the Middle East intensified, even as talks continued between Iran and mediators from Oman and Qatar.

ADNOC L&S of the United Arab Emirates said on Wednesday that one crew member was missing and 11 injured after one of its vessels was attacked in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday.

An LPG tanker was also struck by a projectile off the coast of Oman on Monday, prompting its crew to evacuate the ship.

“Although regional supply may continue to recover through alternative routes, the latest vessel data suggests that normalization of flows through Hormuz is still not possible under current conditions,” LSEG analysts said on Tuesday.

Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis said on Tuesday that they launched five drones toward two pumping stations along Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline, which has been used to bypass the strait.

Saudi Arabia is preparing for the conflict with the Houthis to stretch well into next year, said two Western officials briefed on the plans by Saudi officials.

Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump is expected to hold bilateral talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in China on Thursday, in addition to the trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, US and Russian officials said.

Trump’s envoys have intensified diplomatic efforts to end Russia’s war in Ukraine, with discussions that are also set to involve European leaders focused on post-war security guarantees and economic recovery planning. REUTERS

data.title: The perverse effects of the AI investment boom
data.description:
SOVEREIGN and corporate debt levels have been flashing red for some time.

In the US, federal debt now exceeds 100 per cent of gross domestic product, and the cost of servicing it – US$1 trillion this year – has overtaken defence spending.

And with French public debt reaching roughly 119 per cent of GDP, yields have come under pressure as investors question the sustainability of the country’s fiscal path.

Meanwhile, big technology companies have been borrowing as if there were no tomorrow, both on public markets and through private credit.

The so-called hyperscalers – those investing tens of billions of dollars in AI data centres – had hitherto funded their investments mainly from existing cashflows and equity. But now they are turning increasingly to debt financing.

Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Oracle raised US$194 billion through bonds in the first half of 2026 alone – compared with roughly US$108 billion for all of 2025 – and their combined 2026 issuance is on track to reach US$250 billion.

Moreover, in September, Amazon raised £4.25 billion (US$5.8 billion) through its first-ever sterling-denominated bond, having already tapped the euro and other major bond markets.

The maturities on these recently issued bonds span from three to 19 years, with yields between 5.2 and 6.7 per cent. And separately, Alphabet stretched maturities and issued a 100-year “century” bond earlier in 2026.

This massive AI-driven fundraising has had three immediate consequences.

First, it demonstrates that large US tech companies can easily tap debt markets globally, and in currencies other than the dollar.

Second, the scale of the issuances means that hyperscalers can attract substantial institutional capital.

And third, by issuing long-dated bonds, they are now competing with governments for capital from pension funds and insurers.

The hyperscalers’ combined capital expenditure up to 2028 has been estimated at US$1 trillion or more, the equivalent of 3 per cent of US GDP.

That means their demand for capital will continue to grow. But such demand cannot be met from cashflows and equity alone, nor from the US corporate bond market.

So, as the AI data-centre market matures, its reliance on debt is likely to increase quickly.

Most hyperscalers have balance sheets strong enough to earn higher credit ratings than would normally be the case for corporate debt, meaning AA- and higher.

With little additional perceived risk, their bonds are therefore attractive even compared to risk-free assets such as US ten-year Treasuries or German ten-year Bunds.

But what will this competition for capital mean for other sectors and markets?

One risk is that it could have a crowding-out effect, not only among corporate borrowers but also in sovereign-debt markets, where yields could be pushed up, raising governments’ borrowing costs.

When combined with already-high interest rates, this dynamic could generate adverse spillovers for countries that need capital to finance economic development.

With inflation proving persistent, the US Federal Reserve returned to hiking interest rates in September – the first increase since 2023 – and the European Central Bank recently raised its deposit rate for the second time this year, to 2.5 per cent.

But if rates are poised to stay higher for longer, advanced economies and developing countries alike will have less fiscal space, owing to higher debt-service costs.

And this tightening will come just as political pressures for more public spending are mounting, and as the need for greater investment in environmental sustainability is becoming increasingly evident.

While G7 governments already carry historically high debt, the outlook for developing countries is even bleaker.

They may face a double squeeze, because as external capital becomes scarcer and more expensive, domestic financing costs rise in step, crowding out local investment.

For countries whose access to funding is already constrained, a severe fiscal squeeze or even a debt crisis cannot be ruled out. After all, many developing economies are starting from a weak position.

According to the World Bank, they paid US$741 billion more in principal and interest on their external debt than they received in new financing between 2022 and 2024 – the largest such gap in at least 50 years.

Now, the world’s richest companies could be outbidding the world’s poorest countries for the same pool of savings.

It is too soon to know how far this competition will go, but the scale of capital that AI infrastructure clearly demands warrants greater scrutiny.

Given how little evidence there is that AI is boosting revenue growth or lifting margins outside the tech sector, we could well be witnessing an extraordinarily costly misallocation of capital.

Therefore, AI’s promised gains need to be weighed against those investments (such as in climate change mitigation and adaptation) that may never happen now.

And even if the promised gains are borne out, the costs and benefits are unlikely to be distributed equally, both between and within countries.

These adverse spillovers are not receiving the attention they deserve.

What should be done? The G20, which the United Kingdom will chair from Dec 1, is the ideal forum for any coordinated discussion of AI-related capital flows and their spillovers.

This topic should be high on the agenda, with the aim of understanding these dynamics better and agreeing on a coordinated policy response based on shared data and joint analyses.

At the same time, the international community should scale up financial instruments that provide affordable funding to developing countries.

Guarantees from multilateral development banks can crowd private investors in rather than out, and more lending in local currencies can shield borrowers from exchange-rate risks.

The entire debate about AI has revolved around whether it will boost economic growth. But it would be far more practical to ask: Whose growth, and at whose expense? PROJECT SYNDICATE

The writer is professor and chair in sovereign debt and finance at Sciences Po

data.title: European stocks hit two-week on weak miners, caution ahead of Anthropic IPO
data.description:
EUROPEAN shares fell 1 per cent on Wednesday (Nov 18), weighed down by mining and energy stocks as investors remained cautious ahead of AI company Anthropic’s IPO, a key test of appetite for the sector.

The pan-European Stoxx 600 ended down 1.03 per cent at 644.05 points, its third straight session of losses and its lowest close since Nov 6. All major regional bourses fell, with London’s commodity-heavy FTSE 100 down 1.3 per cent.

The Stoxx 600 is now more than 3 per cent below the record high it reached last week.

Mining stocks led declines, falling 4.7 per cent for their steepest one-day drop since May 15 as copper prices slid to a seven-month low.

Glencore and Aurubis both lost more than 5 per cent.

Oil stocks fell 2.1 per cent, tracking lower crude prices.

“We are waiting for this IPO from Anthropic,” said Alexis Bert, head of cash equity Europe at Marex. “It’s a lot of money that are being raised, draining potentially some liquidity on the market.”

European tech shares ended lower after giving up earlier gains as investors awaited pricing of Anthropic’s IPO later on Wednesday. The company is targeting a valuation of up to US$1.4 trillion.

In the US, the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell as shares of AI heavyweight Nvidia declined after its upbeat forecast failed to ease investor concerns about the AI trade.

European chip equipment maker ASML rose 1.9 per cent but surrendered most of its earlier gains.

Among other stocks, French train maker Alstom fell 7.2 per cent after reporting a net loss of 822 million euros (US$902 million), adding to pressure from a warning earlier this month about certification delays.

Credit data provider Experian gained 1.7 per cent after first-half revenue topped estimates and it announced a US$500 million share buyback.

Puma fell 1 per cent after US rival Nike signalled tougher competition, raising concerns that European sportswear makers could face weaker pricing power as input costs rise in 2027.

Deutsche Bank fell 3.1 per cent, extending a 6 per cent decline from Tuesday after the leak of a large cache of internal records renewed scrutiny of its past dealings.

Separately, Reuters reported that European Central Bank policymakers will discuss next week raising minimum reserve requirements for euro zone banks, a move that would drain liquidity from the financial system and reduce the ECB’s interest bill. REUTERS

data.title: US stocks: Wall Street ends mixed after Nvidia earnings, Fed minutes
data.description:
US STOCKS were mixed on Wednesday (Nov 18) as investors digested Nvidia results ahead of Anthropic’s initial public offering pricing, while weighing hawkish sentiment reflected in US Federal Reserve minutes.

After gyrating early in the session, the Nasdaq closed modestly higher, the Dow ended sharply lower, while the S&P 500 reversed its modest gains to settle in negative territory following the Fed minutes release.

Nvidia’s quarterly results released late on Tuesday beat analyst expectations, and the AI chipmaker forecast quarterly revenue above estimates. Even so, its shares fell amid uncertainties caused by co-founder Jensen Huang’s sudden departure last week.

The Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index, which has handily outperformed the broader market this year, closed slightly lower, underscoring lofty expectations for the sector amid massive spending on AI infrastructure and potential risk associated with the nascent technology.

Anthropic’s IPO is expected to price after the market closes on Wednesday. At the top of its US$70 to US$78 range, the offering would raise about US$64.4 billion and value the company at about US$1.4 trillion.

Other chipmakers were mixed. Intel and Micron lost ground, but Advanced Micro Devices advanced.

“There’s been a lot of dark clouds of uncertainty over technology, chip stocks and AI in general,” said Ryan Detrick, chief market strategist at Carson Group in Omaha. “It’s important to remember the market’s not totally falling apart here. It clearly is top-heavy with tech, but there are other groups that are actually doing pretty well under the surface.”

Target jumped 4 per cent after the discount retailer provided an upbeat holiday outlook. Results from its larger rival Walmart are expected on Thursday.

TJX surged 8 per cent after forecasting strong annual sales, banking on high demand ahead of the holiday shopping season.

Take-Two Interactive shares rose 6.2 per cent ahead of the rollout of its Grand Theft Auto VI video game.

On the sector level, consumer discretionary was a clear outperformer, with a boost from a 3.8 per cent gain in Amazon shares.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 561.25 points, or 1.11 per cent, to 50,198.17, the S&P 500 lost 16.89 points, or 0.23 per cent, to 7,323.64 and the Nasdaq Composite gained 101.50 points, or 0.42 per cent, to 24,429.89.

Focus on the Fed

Minutes from the Fed’s October policy meeting showed the central bank remained focused on inflation risks, recognising the need for further rate hikes if the economy progresses as expected. A few policymakers argued the case for a 50-basis-point rate hike “if incoming inflation data were unfavourable.”

Consumer and producer price data released after the October meeting showed hotter-than-expected price growth.

Fed Governor Christopher Waller took a hawkish stance on Wednesday, saying the central bank needs to be more aggressive in responding to inflation. This follows John Williams’ comments on Tuesday, in which the New York Fed president said that while he favours tighter monetary policy, there was no need for “dramatic action.”

Financial markets are pricing in a near-certain probability of a 25-basis-point interest rate hike at the conclusion of the Fed’s December meeting, according to CME’s FedWatch tool.

“Inflation continues to be stubbornly higher than anyone wants,” Detrick said. “The Fed’s going to probably do a 25-basis-point hike in December, and a couple more hikes early next year is a very real possibility.”

Housing data released on Wednesday showed mortgage rates climbing, building permits faltering, and pending home sales dropping to a record low. REUTERS

data.title: US mortgage rates rise for the first time in five weeks
data.description:
US MORTGAGE rates rose for the first time in five weeks, halting a nascent rebound in home-purchase activity and clouding an already gloomy outlook for housing. 

The contract rate on a 30-year fixed mortgage climbed 14 basis points to 7.37.35 per cent the week ended Nov 13, according to data released on Wednesday (Nov 18) by the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA).

The increase snaps a stretch of weekly declines that helped yield a modest pickup in home-purchase applications. Borrowing costs now stand nearly a full percentage point higher than a year ago.

An index of loan applications for home purchases slipped 2.5 per cent, marking the ninth weekly decline since the end of August. MBA’s refinance gauge fell 1.5 per cent, the first decrease in four weeks. 

A rapid escalation in financing costs in September into early October briefly brought mortgage rates to 7.5 per cent, punishing the housing market.

Contract signings in the home resale market reached a record low in September, and this month an index of home-builder sentiment fell to its lowest level in 14 years.

Multi-family dwellings up

Still, home-builders started more homes in October, driven largely by a rebound in apartment construction while the single-family market remained challenged by high mortgage rates.

Housing starts increased 9.9 per cent to an annualised rate of 1.31 million, the fastest in three months. Economists surveyed by Bloomberg expected a 1.25 million pace, based on the median projection.

New construction of multi-family dwellings rose nearly 24 per cent. Starts of single-family homes increased 4 per cent to an annualised rate of 864,000.

Despite the October increase, the pace of single-family home construction remains near the slowest this year. Permits for houses slumped to the lowest since 2023, suggesting home-builders are waiting out a period of over-7 per cent mortgage rates and consumers’ worries about affordability.

Economists see the new-home market as stagnant at best until borrowing costs drop. The Federal National Mortgage Association, widely known as Fannie Mae, sees housing starts barely improving through at least the end of 2028.

In an earnings call with analysts last month, builder PulteGroup noted its progress in reducing its share of “spec homes”, or homes built without a buyer in mind. Such homes can find quick buyers in strong market, but can require more sales incentives in slower times.

DR Horton, which targets many first-time buyers, is building more smaller homes lately, including duplexes and town houses.

Meanwhile, total building permits, which point to future construction, decreased 7.4 per cent last month to an annualised 1.3 million, the weakest since May 2020.

GDP impact

Once a solid contributor to the US’ economy, home construction has been a drag the last two years, weighing on gross domestic product for six of the past seven quarters.

Before the latest starts data, the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta’s GDPNow forecast showed residential investment may again subtract from growth in the fourth quarter.

By region, housing starts rose in the Midwest and the South. New construction in the South, the nation’s biggest home-building region, was the strongest since April. In the West, starts fell to the lowest level in more than six years.

The new residential construction data is volatile, and the government report showed 90 per cent confidence that the monthly change ranged from a 6.9 per cent decline to a 26.7 per cent gain. BLOOMBERG
